text: But there are other stories that are not about catastrophe. <break time="0.8s" /> And it is very important, it is just as important, to talk about them. <break time="0.8s" /> I have always felt that it is impossible to engage properly with a place or a person without engaging with all of the stories of that place and that person. <break time="0.8s" /> The consequence of the single story is this, it robs people of dignity. <break time="0.8s" /> It makes our recognition of our equal humanity difficult. <break time="0.8s" /> It emphasizes how we are different rather than how we are similar. <break time="0.8s" /> So what if before my Mexican trip I had followed the immigration debate from both sides, the U, S, and the Mexican. <break time="0.8s" /> What if my mother had told us that Fides family was poor and hardworking. <break time="0.8s" /> What if we had an African television network that broadcast diverse African stories all over the world. <break time="0.8s" /> What the Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe calls a balance of stories. <break time="0.8s" /> What if my roommate knew about my Nigerian publisher, Mukta Bakaray, a remarkable man who left his job in a bank to follow his dream and start a publishing house. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, the conventional wisdom was that Nigerians do not read literature. <break time="0.8s" /> He disagreed. <break time="0.8s" /> He felt that people who could read, would read, if you made literature affordable and available to them. <break time="0.8s" /> Shortly after he published my first novel I went to a TV station in Lagos to do an interview. <break time="0.8s" /> And a woman who worked there as a messenger came up to me and said, I really liked your novel, I did not like the ending, Now you must write a sequel, and this is what will happen. <break time="0.8s" /> And she went on to tell me what to write in the sequel. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, I was not only charmed, I was very moved. <break time="0.8s" /> Here was a woman, part of the ordinary masses of Nigerians, who were not supposed to be readers. <break time="0.8s" /> She had not only read the book, but she had taken ownership of it and felt justified in telling me what to write in the sequel. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, what if my roommate knew about my friend Funmi Iyanda, a fearless woman who hosts a TV show in Lagos, and is determined to tell the stories that we prefer to forget. <break time="0.8s" /> What if my roommate knew about the heart procedure that was performed in the Lagos hospital last week.
